'''Krithi Karanth''' is a [[conservation biologist]] who is chief conservation scientist and director at the [[Centre for Wildlife Studies]] (CWS), [[Bangalore]], [[India]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Centre for Wildlife Studies – CWS India - Centre for Wildlife Studies |url=https://cwsindia.org/ |website=CWS India |access-date=29 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="Explorer">{{cite web |title=Explorer Home |url=https://explorers.nationalgeographic.org/directory/krithi-k-karanth |website=explorers.nationalgeographic.org |access-date=29 August 2025 |language=en}}</ref> and an adjunct faculty member of the Nicholas School at [[Duke University]] in the United States and the [[National Centre for Biological Sciences]] in India.<ref name="NGI">{{cite news |title=Krithi Karanth: Finding the balance between human communities and nature |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/impact/article/krithi-karanth-human-communities-nature |access-date=29 August 2025 |work=Impact |publisher=National Geographic |date=29 August 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

Karanth is a [[National Geographic Explorer]],<ref name="Zhu" /> and has received multiple awards for her research, conservation and educational work, including the 2025 John P. McNulty Prize and the 2019 [[Women of Discovery Awards]].  She was the first Indian and Asian woman to receive the 2021 Wild Innovator Award.<ref name="Thakur" /> This award from the Wild Elements Foundation is given to innovators, advocates and partners to "disrupt the status quo and identify solutions to global sustainability and conservation".<ref name="Wild"/>

==Early life and education==
Krithi Karanth grew up in [[Karnataka|Karnataka, India]], in the [[Western Ghats]], where her father, conservation biologist [[K. Ullas Karanth]] studies tigers.<ref name="Thakur" /><ref name="Zhu" />  She saw her first tiger on a field trip at the age of three.<ref name="Thakur" />  At a young age, she learned how to track tigers and to set camera traps.<ref name="Thakur" /><ref name="Zhu">{{cite news |last1=Zhu |first1=Melissa |title=Krithi Karanth inspires human-wildlife connection for Indian youth, and beyond |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/impact/article/krithi-karanth-explorer-story |access-date=29 August 2025 |work=Impact |publisher=National Geographic |date=29 August 2025 |language=en}}</ref> Her mother Prathibha Karanth worked as a professor at the SRC Institute of Speech and Hearing, Bangalore.<ref name="Sanjeevi" />

Karanth has a B.S (Environmental Science) and B.A degrees (Geography) from the [[University of Florida]] (2001), a Master's in Environmental Science (M.E.Sc) from [[Yale University]] (2003), and a Ph.D in Environmental Science and Policy from [[Duke University]] (2008).<ref>{{cite web |title=Mongabay’s Interview with Krithi Karanth, Wildlife Scientist |url=https://www.conservationindia.org/articles/mongabays-interview-with-krithi-karanth-wildlife-scientist |website=Conservation India |access-date=29 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="Hance">{{cite news |last1=Hance |first1=Jeremy |title=Parks key to saving India’s great mammals from extinction |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2011/0224-hance_karanth.html/ |access-date=29 August 2025 |work=Mongabay |date=24 Feb 2011}}</ref> Karanth did postdoctoral work at [[Columbia University|Columbia University]]  from 2009-2010.<ref name="Rego"/><ref name="Lobo">{{cite news |last1=Lobo |first1=Joanna |date=September 24, 2023 |title=The Wild World of Krithi Karanth {{!}} Roundglass Sustain {{!}} Roundglass {{!}} Sustain |url=https://roundglasssustain.com/heroes/krithi-karanth |access-date=29 August 2025 |work=roundglasssustain.com |language=en}}</ref> In her doctoral thesis, Karanth studied the extinction of species of large mammals in India. This work was published in ''[[Proceedings of the Royal Society|Proceedings of The Royal Society of London]]'' in 2010.<ref name="Sanjeevi" />

==Work==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_WONasjws4&ab_channel=Indiaspora “Ted Style Talk: Dr. Krithi Karanth, CEO, Center for Wildlife Studies & National Geographic Explorer”], Indiaspora, April 11, 2024 |video2= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qhFCCrWvy1A&ab_channel=ExploringByTheSeatOfYourPants Krithi Karanth, Rewilding India: Transforming Human-Wildlife Interactions], May 27, 2021}}

At age 31, Karanth returned to India, becoming a Ramanujan Fellow and a research fellow at the Centre for Wildlife Studies (CWS India).<ref name="Thakur" /> Through research in India and Asia, Karanth examines interactions between humans and wildlife, and their impacts on conservation. She studies patterns of species distributions and extinction and the impacts of activities such as wildlife tourism, voluntary resettlement, biodiversity in production landscapes, and changes in land use patterns.<ref name="Zhu" /><ref name="Coxon">{{cite news |last1=Coxon |first1=Cheyenne |title=NCEAS Portrait: Krithi Karanth is Reducing Human-Wildlife Conflict with Improved Data Accessibility and Use |url=https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/news/nceas-portrait-krithi-karanth |access-date=29 August 2025 |work=National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis |date=December 18, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> Her research work on resettlement has been used as a basis for Central government policy decisions. Her research on tourism was presented as evidence in a Supreme Court case that reviewed guidelines for national wildlife tourism.<ref name="Sanjeevi" />

In 2015, Karanth founded "Wild Seve" (“wild service” in [[Kannada]]), providing a helpline and staff to help people register and process claims for government compensation for wild animal-caused losses to crops, livestock or property.  Staff members attempt to follow up on reports within 48 hours, to document damage and file paperwork. They then track the claim until it is paid out. Large mammals such as leopards and wolves may attack livestock or people; wild pigs can damage crops; and elephants may also damage property. As of 2021, the Wild Seve program had processed nearly 18,000 claims from the 600 villages and settlements near the Bandipur and Nagarhole national parks. In 2018, CWS worked with the [[Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy]] to review the government compensation policies of various regions and recommend best practices.<ref name="Rego">{{Cite web |last=Rego |first=Natasha |date=May 7, 2021 |title=Peace-keeping force: Krithi Karanth wins award for work on human-animal conflict |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/lifestyle/art-culture/peacekeeping-force-krithi-karanth-wins-award-for-work-on-human-animal-conflict-101620400442419.html |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=Hindustan Times |language=en}}</ref>   

Children, particularly those living near wildlife reserves, are likely to first experience wild animals as causes of damage to people, crops, and livestock. This can be traumatic and  result in significant economic hardship.<ref name="Thakur" />  In 2017, Karanth began working with educator Gabby Salazar to develop a "conservation program that uses education, art, storytelling, and games"<ref name="Zhu" />  to help local populations, particularly students, who may come into frequent contact with wildlife.  Students learn to better understand wild animals that they may encounter in their habitats, and develop strategies to respond in ways that can minimize conflict. Their first program was "Wild Shaale" (“wild school” in  [[Kannada]]). Piloted in 2018 in 38 classes, the program has since been used in hundreds of schools and reached over 30,000 children.<ref name="Zhu" /><ref name="Thakur" />

In 2020 Karanth began the program  "Wild Surakshe" (“wild health” in Kannada) to address health issues affecting national parks and protected areas in Karnataka. Examples of such concerns include first-aid, cases of rabies and leptospirosis, and Nipah virus outbreaks.<ref name="Rego" />    

Karanth has published more than 100 articles<ref name=":1" /> and been on the editorial boards of the journals ''[[Conservation Biology (journal)|Conservation Biology]]'', ''[[Conservation Letters]]'', and ''[[Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment]]''. She has involved and supervised over 200 scientists and 750 [[citizen science]] volunteers in the course of her research and conservation work.<ref name="Explorer" /> 

Her work has been covered nationally and internationally. Her research and conservation work have been featured in the BBC Series ''The Hunt'' (2015) by [[David Attenborough]], ''Big Cats'' (2018)  and ''Dynasties'' (2018), and in documentaries by CBC and PBS.<ref name=":0" /> Karanth has co-produced the documentaries ''Wild Seve'' (2017),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mantri |first=Geetika |date=2017-03-30 |title=Laws of the jungle: B'luru filmmaker's documentary on human-animal conflict is going places |url=https://www.thenewsminute.com/karnataka/laws-jungle-bluru-filmmakers-documentary-human-animal-conflict-going-places-59521 |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=The News Minute |language=en}}</ref> ''Humane Highways (2018),''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dattatri |first=Shekar |date=20 December 2018 |title=Shekar Dattatri: From Killer Roads To Humane Highways {{!}} Nature inFocus |url=https://www.natureinfocus.in/environment/quick-five-shekar-dattatri |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=www.natureinfocus.in |language=en}}</ref> ''Wild Shaale,''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Salazar |first=Gabby |date=2024-08-05 |title=Wild Shaale: Bringing India’s Wild Wonders into the Classroom |url=https://blog.education.nationalgeographic.org/2024/08/05/wild-shaale-bringing-indias-wild-wonders-into-the-classroom/ |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=National Geographic Education Blog |language=en-US}}</ref> ''Flying Elephants'' (2020, with Prakash Matada)<ref name="Gomes">{{cite news |last1=Gomes |first1=Suruchi Kapur |title=Krithi Karanth: Polymath with a mission |url=https://latest.sundayguardianlive.com/culture/krithi-karanth-polymath-mission |access-date=29 August 2025 |work=Sunday Guardian Live |date=October 24, 2020}}</ref> and ''Wild Surakshe'' (2020).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Krithi Karanth |url=https://wingswomenofdiscovery.org/explorer/karanth/ |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=WINGS Women of Discovery |language=en-US}}</ref> Karanth appeared with [[Kevin Pietersen]] in ''Save This Rhino: India'' ''(2020),'' produced by Disney Hotstar and National Geographic.<ref name=":0" />
